name: Many Black Holes and Wormholes in Three Dimensions
short_name: Many Black Holes and Wormholes in Three Dimensions
description: Anti-de Sitter space of three dimensions cut along timelike surfaces and glued back together, which makes any number of black holes joined behind their horizons, or one black hole with a wormhole of any genus inside it. Every exterior is that of a Bañados-Teitelboim-Zanelli black hole, and the whole spacetime is drawn on Poincaré's disc.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit. Each chart covers a part of anti-de Sitter space of radius $\ell$, and the spacetime is the region of it between timelike surfaces that are identified in pairs.
history: In three dimensions a black hole can be built by cutting anti-de Sitter space and gluing the edges [banados1993]. Gravity there has no waves and does not vary from place to place: with a negative cosmological constant $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$, empty spacetime has the curvature of anti-de Sitter space at every point, beside a black hole as much as far from it [brill2000]. The hole that Máximo Bañados, Claudio Teitelboim, and Jorge Zanelli found in 1992 is, as they showed with Marc Henneaux a year later, anti-de Sitter space with some of its points declared the same [banados1992, banados1993]. At the hole's moment of rest, space is a strip of the hyperbolic plane between two straight lines that stay apart all the way to infinity, with its two edges glued together, and the shortest loop around the resulting funnel is the horizon, of length $2\pi\sqrt{M}\,\ell$ for a hole of mass $M$ [brill1996]. What do more cuts make?¶The answer came from the University of Maryland in November 1995, where Dieter Brill drew three such lines, no two of them meeting, and kept the region between them [brill1996]. He laid a second copy of the region on top of the first and sewed the two together along all three edges, a step he called doubling [brill1996]. The seams close up into a pair of trousers whose waist and legs flare out to infinity, and the narrowest loop around each of the three is a horizon [brill1996, brill2000]. Beyond its loop each flare is exactly the outside of a black hole of Bañados, Teitelboim, and Zanelli, and with $n$ lines the $n$ outsides "join in one 'interior' region" that "acts as a closed universe containing $n$ black holes" [brill1996]. Alan Steif, at the University of California at Davis, had found the same construction on his own and posted it twelve days after Brill, and each added a note to his paper crediting the other [brill1996, steif1996]. Steif said what it means for anyone watching from outside: in an open universe "two black holes cannot exist separately, but are necessarily enclosed by a third horizon" [steif1996].¶Once the moment of rest has passed, do the holes stay apart? Freely falling observers in anti-de Sitter space fall toward one another, and the cut surfaces are swept out by such observers starting from rest, so the surfaces close in on the region between them [brill2000]. Brill followed those observers and found the inside shrinking around them, the holes approaching one another as "test particles in a background adS space" would [brill1996]. All of them, wherever they start, reach the end after the same proper time, $\pi\ell/2c$ [brill2000]. Just before it, in Brill's words, space "looks like $n$ thin horns that flare out at infinity and are connected on their thin ends" [brill1996]. The end is a singularity of the kind Charles Misner described in 1967, with no curvature growing large: the glued surfaces cross there, and the spacetime "fails to be Hausdorff" [brill1996, misner1967].¶Sewing the two legs of the trousers to each other leaves one flare, the waist, with a handle behind its horizon [aminneborg1998]. This black hole dates from 1997, when Brill worked with four physicists in Stockholm, Stefan Åminneborg, Ingemar Bengtsson, Sören Holst, and Peter Peldán, and with more trousers they gave it an inside of any genus from one up [aminneborg1998]. They drew it in a chart where every moment of time is Poincaré's disc and the whole of anti-de Sitter space is a solid cylinder, sausage coordinates by name [aminneborg1998, brill2000]. In that picture the cut surfaces lean together like the sides of a tent, and the black hole is the part of the tent that cannot be seen from its openings [aminneborg1998]. These are, in their words, "non-eternal black holes with collapsing wormhole topologies": the spacetime begins at a singularity in its past, and the event horizon is born later, at a point in the middle, and spreads outward [aminneborg1998].¶Can anyone outside tell that the handle is there? A theorem of 1993, due to John Friedman, Kristin Schleich, and Donald Witt, says of spacetimes that are flat far away that "general relativity does not allow an observer to probe the topology of spacetime" [friedman1993]. Anti-de Sitter space lies outside their assumptions, so the five authors checked by hand: a trip from one opening of the tent across to the opposite one takes a sausage time of $\pi\ell/c$, and no opening lasts that long [aminneborg1998]. Looking still works, since two rays of light from one event on the axis of the tent, before the horizon is born, reach infinity through different openings, one round each side of the handle [aminneborg1998]. So "we can see the full extent of the wormhole from infinity, even though we cannot travel through it" [aminneborg1998].¶Brill set the family out in lectures on Samos in 1998, and while there proved the theorem of Pythagoras, "a local boy who contributed to the early fame of Samos", by cutting and tiling the plane as he cuts and tiles the disc [brill2000]. A spacetime with $k$ outsides and $g$ handles, by his count, has $6g + 3k - 6$ free numbers at its moment of rest: the lengths of its loops and the twists with which they are sewn [brill2000]. Holography gave the many outsides a use, since there entanglement between field theories on the boundaries goes with a connection through the inside [balasubramanian2014]. By 2009 these wormholes had a holographic description, from Kostas Skenderis and Balt van Rees, with a state of the boundary theories "capturing the non-trivial topology behind the horizons" [skenderis2011]. Five years on, Vijay Balasubramanian, Patrick Hayden, Alexander Maloney, Donald Marolf, and Simon Ross took the hole with $n$ outsides as the dual of $n$ entangled field theories, and found wormholes for which "there is intrinsic entanglement between all $n$ parties" [balasubramanian2014].

related.text: Outside each horizon the spacetime is exactly the exterior of a BTZ black hole without rotation. One pair of glued surfaces alone makes that hole whole [brill1996].
Every point of these spacetimes has a neighbourhood that is anti-de Sitter space of three dimensions. They differ from it only in which points count as the same [brill1996, aminneborg1998].

Glue the two edges of a wedge of the hyperbolic plane and you get a point particle where the strip between two lines gives a black hole. Steif put particles and holes on the same disc and found when a horizon forms around them [steif1996].

The same construction in four dimensions, by four of the same authors. Åminneborg, Bengtsson, Holst, and Peldán identified points of anti-de Sitter space there and got horizons of genus two or more [aminneborg1996].

A black hole with one exterior and a topology of its own behind the horizon, made from Schwarzschild's spacetime by an identification. Åminneborg and his coauthors gave it as the example of such a hole in four dimensions [aminneborg1998, friedman1993].

A moment of rest holding many black holes in four dimensions. There two holes may or may not share an outer horizon, and in three dimensions with an open universe they always do [brill1996, steif1996].
The moment of rest of one hole is a bridge between two outsides, which Steif set beside Einstein and Rosen's. With three or more outsides the bridge becomes a junction [steif1996, brill1996].
Minkowski space identified under a boost. These spacetimes end where their glued surfaces cross, in a singularity of Misner's kind with the curvature finite [brill1996, misner1967].

Sören Holst put Gott's time machine in anti-de Sitter space using the chart in which these spacetimes are drawn, with Poincaré's disc at every moment. With Hans-Jürgen Matschull he showed that the pair of particles there is a rotating BTZ hole [holst1996, holst1999].

coordinates.name: Sausage

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$

coordinates.convention: We use sausage coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ a length, in which every moment of $t$ is Poincaré's disc of radius $\ell$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Stereographic

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$

coordinates.convention: We use stereographic coordinates $(\tau, x, y)$, with $\tau$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$ and $y$ lengths, centred on the event $\tau = x = y = 0$ at which the identified surfaces meet. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{\tau} + \dfrac{2c\,\tau}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{\tau}^2 - \dfrac{4x}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{\tau}\dot{x} - \dfrac{4y}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{\tau}\dot{y} + \dfrac{2c\,\tau}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{x}^2 + \dfrac{2c\,\tau}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{y}^2 = 0

\ddot{x} - \dfrac{2x}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{\tau}^2 + \dfrac{4c\,\tau}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{\tau}\dot{x} - \dfrac{2x}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{x}^2 - \dfrac{4y}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{x}\dot{y} + \dfrac{2x}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{y}^2 = 0

\ddot{y} - \dfrac{2y}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{\tau}^2 + \dfrac{4c\,\tau}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{\tau}\dot{y} + \dfrac{2y}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{x}^2 - \dfrac{4x}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{x}\dot{y} - \dfrac{2y}{x^2 + y^2 - c^2\,\tau^2 - 4\ell^2}\dot{y}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Free Fall

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(T, \rho, \phi)$, with $T$ the proper time of the observers who fall freely from rest at the moment of time symmetry $T = 0$, and $\rho$ and $\phi$ their place on Poincaré's disc at that moment. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cT$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{T}$ means $d(cT)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Exterior

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$

Mass of the black hole seen from one exterior, dimensionless, $M = 8Gm/c^2$ for a hole of mass $m$, with $G$ Newton's constant in three dimensions; its horizon is a circle of length $2\pi\sqrt{M}\,\ell$

coordinates.convention: We use Schwarzschild coordinates $(t, r, \phi)$ outside one horizon, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $2\pi r$ the length of a circle of $\phi$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
